A guy was about to tap "Buy Now" on a $299.99 espresso machine on Amazon. Full price.

His wife, a former Amazon fulfillment operations lead, took the phone out of his hands.

She scrolled 3 inches down the exact same product page. Tapped one small gray link. Same machine. Same brand. Same model. Shipped from the same Amazon warehouse. $164.19.

"How?"

"Look at the fulfillment tag. See where it says Amazon Resale: Like New? That means the outer cardboard box got dented on a delivery pallet. The $299.99 is the standard retail listing. The $164.19 is the exact same unopened machine inside a bruised box. Same return protection. Same two-day Prime truck. $135 difference. Because you only look at the yellow Buy Now button."

He looked at her.

"How long have you known this?"

"Since my first week at the fulfillment center. 5 years ago. Everything on Amazon runs on warehouse codes and pricing triggers. LPN stickers track returns. The 15th of the month forces sellers into liquidation. A simple URL code unlocks hidden 70% clearance. I've been using them for years. You've been paying retail for years."

Here's every hidden Amazon warehouse code and pricing rule and what it means for your wallet:

Code 1: "Used - Like New" under Amazon Resale. Brand new products trapped in dented cardboard at up to 40% off retail.

She said this is the single biggest pricing loophole on the entire platform, because most shoppers see the word "Used" and immediately scroll past it.

"Right below the yellow 'Buy Now' button on millions of items, there is a small box that says 'Save with Used - Like New' sold by Amazon Resale, formerly called Amazon Warehouse. Most buyers assume someone used the product at home and sent it back dirty. In the vast majority of cases for 'Like New' grade, that's completely false."

"Inside an Amazon fulfillment center, strict platform compliance rules dictate what can be sold as 'New.' If a forklift bumps a pallet and crushes the corner of a cardboard box, that item is dead as 'New' inventory. If a customer orders the wrong color, opens the outer shipping tape, sees their mistake, and drops it at UPS without ever touching the product inside, it cannot go back into the 'New' bin."

"Instead, a warehouse associate runs a quick visual grading check, sees the factory plastic seal is still intact, grades it 'Used - Like New,' and the pricing system automatically slashes the price by 25% to 50% to clear the shelf space."

"She said 'Used - Like New' and 'Used - Very Good' are how employees furnish their entire homes. 'When I worked the grading station, I watched brand-new $400 kitchen appliances, Sony headphones, and power tools get marked down by $150 simply because the cardboard box had a tear from a box cutter. The machine inside had never been plugged into a wall. Shoppers who click the yellow button pay an extra $135 just to have unwrinkled cardboard that they throw in the recycling bin ten minutes after delivery.'"

Code 2: The "LPN" Barcode Sticker. The warehouse License Plate Number that gives you instant leverage when a "New" item isn't new.

She said this three-letter code is printed on a small white sticker on millions of packages, and knowing what it means gives you immediate leverage with customer support.

"Every single item that passes through an Amazon return center gets slapped with a white barcode sticker starting with the letters 'LPN,' which stands for License Plate Number. That sticker ties the physical box to a specific return ID in Amazon's internal database, recording the return history of that exact unit."

"Here is why you need to check every box you order: fulfillment center workers move fast under intense hourly quotas. Mistakes happen constantly. A returned item with an LPN sticker occasionally gets routed back into the 'New' inventory bin by mistake."

"If you pay full retail price for a 'New' item and it arrives with a white LPN barcode sticker stuck over the original manufacturer barcode, you did not receive untouched factory inventory. You paid full price for a previously returned unit."

"When this happens, you don't have to pack it up and drive to UPS. Open the Amazon customer chat and use the exact warehouse terminology. Tell the agent: 'I paid full retail price for a New item, but the package arrived with an LPN return sticker on the box. Since I received previously returned inventory, I would like an open-box partial credit adjustment to keep it instead of returning it.'"

"She said mentioning the LPN code changes the chat conversation immediately. 'The moment you point out the LPN sticker, the support rep knows a fulfillment grading error happened. Because it costs Amazon money to ship that item back and re-grade it, support agents can offer a partial refund or promotional credit on the spot so you keep the item without triggering a return.'"

Information about the significant incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright continues to be limited. A quick summary of what is currently known for those checking in this morning:

An incident occurred at CFB Wainwright, about two hours East of Edmonton, yesterday that has resulted in fatalities and injuries and led to a significant response by local and provincial emergency services, the CAF, and the Government of Canada.

The incident involved a fire that started in the training area of CFB Wainwright around 4pm local time, and quickly spread due (in part) to high winds. The fire spread outside the base fence line to the South, and did not enter the town of Wainwright itself. Over night, officials confirmed that the fire was now "held".

This information has been provided directly through DND's or the Municipal District of Wainwright's official channels and can be treated as likely reliable, although even official sources sometimes get specific information incorrect initially.

Multiple media sources are reporting that the incident has overwhelmed local health care services and improvised sites (ie. The local school) are being used as part of providing medical care. Multiple hospitals in Edmonton have received or are expecting patients and have initiated mass casualty protocols that include asking local residents to seek care through other avenues where possible due to capacity limitations. These appear to be reliable indicators that the even has a high number of casualties.

I can find evidence in Edmonton of similar protocols being activated for incidents involving ~20 significant injuries, but not at as many facilities. I would suggest that figure can, therefore, be treated as a likely floor for the number of serious injuries that are being transported to Edmonton in relation to this incident. That is my analysis and should not be treated as fact without further confirmation.

Global News began reporting over night that at least seven individuals were killed, and dozens were injured in an explosion that initiated this incident. They are also reporting that the explosion was caused by live-fire training that hit a gas line or gas well which appear confirmed to exist on the base (though it's less clear what exists in the precise area of the incident). Global News attributes this information to multiple unnamed sources.

Global News a major media outlet with institutional editorial standards, however, it's notable that other major news organization are not reporting this except by referencing Global News directly. It seems unlikely that Global News has been uniquely able to speak to unnamed sources, suggesting this information is on the fringe of meeting reporting standards. It should be taken seriously, but also treated cautiously until independently confirmed.

Multiple air ambulance type aircraft have been tracked arriving in Wainwright since the incident, and various videos showing multiple conventional ambulances responding are also circulating. These appear to be genuine reports, however, the exact significance of the scale of of the response is somewhat open to interpretation. This should be treated as raw data that requires careful interpretation.

A C-130 aircraft from Winnipeg, using identification information that matches an aircraft belonging to 435 Search and Rescue Squadron was tracked last night heading towards Wainwright. This should also be treated as raw data.

On the ground reporting indicates that a number of CAF personnel parachuted into the area near the hospital. This would align, somewhat, with the C-130 flight, as the aircraft can deploy SAR Techs, who are high readiness personnel with significant medical expertise, this way.

*In an earlier version of this post I suggested treating these reports as possible but suspect. However, there appears to be at least one still-photo image of a person in the air under a canopy from the incident. I would therefore amend that evaluation and call this reporting likely.*

I have seen some discussion of the specific unit(s) involved in the incident. While I have high confidence that publicly available information provides this information, I'd discourage everyone from naming a unit until this is officially confirmed. Allow notification processes to take place, please.

That's the morning update based on what I can confirm. I will attempt to monitor the situation throughout the day and provide updates, but I am doing this independently without support or compensation -- it's possible I may be slower than other sources in order to meet the level of confirmation I believe it appropriate before sharing information.

Many people judge candidates and policies by a single deciding feature, new research suggests | Eric W. Dolan, PsyPost

When people make complex political decisions, they tend to rely on simple mental shortcuts rather than exhaustively weighing every piece of information, according to a study published in PNAS. The research indicates that people frequently switch between different decision strategies depending on the issue at hand and the complexity of the choice environment. These findings suggest that standard survey methods in political science, which often assume people act as fully thorough evaluators, may obscure how individuals actually reach conclusions.

Social scientists frequently rely on choice-based conjoint experiments to measure public opinion on complex topics. In this type of survey, participants view side-by-side profiles of two options, such as hypothetical political candidates or policy proposals, with features that vary randomly, such as age, profession, or cost. Participants are then asked to pick the option they prefer, allowing researchers to infer how much specific features sway voter preferences on average across the entire population.

A key open question is whether people answering these multi-feature surveys actually weigh every detail, as many standard analysis methods implicitly assume, or rely on simplifying mental shortcuts known as heuristics. Some evidence points toward shortcuts. A 2020 eye-tracking study found that when survey tables included more features and options, people looked at a smaller fraction of the information on screen. In the consumer realm, a 2009 study found that although standard models assume people balance every feature against the others, a sizable minority of participants were better described by rules that rank features and decide based on the most important one.

Similar rankings appear in politics: a 2024 study of candidate choice found that voters tend to focus on party affiliation first, weighing traits like gender or race mainly when two candidates share the same party. Separately, research covered by PsyPost in 2026 found that voters often use left and right political labels as shortcuts to guess where candidates stand.

To understand the cognitive rules guiding these choices, study authors Nidhi V. Banavar, a postdoctoral scholar in the Travers Department of Political Science at the University of California, Berkeley, and Kirk Bansak, also of the University of California, Berkeley, created a mathematical framework to classify individual decision strategies. Their model analyzes a person’s survey selections to infer what attributes matter to them, which values they favor, and which cognitive rule best accounts for their behavior.

“We were interested in the question of how people go about making political choices,” Banavar told PsyPost. “When we estimate complex constructs like political attitudes, a lot of analysis methods implicitly assume that people weigh everything in front of them. We wanted to test whether that was true, and if not, to find how they were deciding instead.”

“This connects to a broader issue, which is that most political attitude research is done at the aggregate level,” Banavar explained. “The aggregate is perfect for giving us the high level snapshot and, for better or for worse, collapses a lot of the variation we see in people: both in terms of their actual preferences and in terms of how they make choices based on those preferences. We were interested in uncollapsing the aggregate and so built a model and designed experiments to do so.”

The model examines four distinct decision strategies that differ in cognitive demand. The most thorough strategy, known as Weighted Additive, involves a rational calculation where an individual weighs every single attribute and sums them up to pick the highest-scoring option. A simpler shortcut strategy, known as Tally, involves counting how many preferred traits each option possesses and choosing the profile with the higher count, without worrying about which traits matter more.

The simplest shortcut rule, called Take The Best, directs a person to choose based solely on whichever single feature matters most to them; they only examine a second feature if the options are tied on their favorite trait. The fourth classification, Contaminant, captures random guessing equivalent to a coin flip.

The scientists evaluated this model across two experiments involving 3,762 American adults recruited through Prolific, with quotas matching national demographics for age, sex, and political affiliation. Participants completed 90 choices divided into three blocks of 30 decisions across three common political topics: selecting between two hypothetical immigrants seeking admission to the United States, choosing between two Senate primary candidates, and choosing between two national climate policy packages. Each option varied across six attributes that each had two possible values.

In the first experiment, which included 1,964 participants, the researchers altered the complexity of the profiles by testing whether allowing ties changed how people decided. Half of the participants saw profiles where traits were never identical between the two options, while the other half saw profiles that contained one to three matching features, such as both candidates being in their 50s. This design was intended to test whether forcing people to look beyond their top attribute would push them toward more thorough evaluation strategies.

The results showed that the simplest shortcut rule, Take The Best, was the most common strategy across all three political domains. In the condition without ties, about 54% of participants were classified as using this single-attribute rule, while roughly 30% were classified as using the rational Weighted Additive strategy, and about 14% used the Tally strategy. When ties were introduced, forcing people to scan deeper into the profiles, use of the Take The Best rule dropped to roughly 45%, while rational strategy use increased to about 40%. Across both conditions, shortcut strategies accounted for the majority of participant behavior.

The authors also discovered that an individual’s strategy was not fixed. Depending on the condition, 67% to 76% of participants were classified as using different strategies for different issues, with about 10% using a completely different strategy across all three domains. The presentation order of the topics was randomized, and participants did not display signs of survey fatigue or increased guessing in later rounds. Instead, people appeared to adapt their decision rules to the specific context of each topic.

“On one hand, the big takeaway is the prevalence of heuristic use and how the majority of individuals use informational shortcuts,” Banavar noted. “This is an important finding – people are not exhaustively weighting and evaluating all the information presented to them.”

“However, I think a bigger takeaway is that people tend to use different strategies depending on the political domain,” Banavar added. “How someone processes information is not a trait: just because I may choose a candidate based on one factor doesn’t mean that I’ll choose a climate policy based on one factor. This means we shouldn’t put people into buckets based on how they make political choices.”

In the second experiment, which included 1,798 participants, the researchers tested another common variation in survey design: asking participants to rate each profile individually on a 1-to-7 scale in addition to making their comparative choice. Among those asked to give ratings, fewer participants were classified as using Take The Best in all three policy domains, though it remained the most common strategy. That group also had more people classified as using the more thorough strategies, along with a small increase in people classified as random guessers, which the authors suggest may reflect some respondents losing interest. The authors caution that these shifts were not consistently statistically reliable across domains.

To check whether these classifications reflected something about how people were actually thinking, rather than just statistical patterns in their choices, the researchers analyzed response times. Participants classified as using the rational Weighted Additive strategy took the longest to answer, followed by those classified as using Tally, while those classified as using Take The Best responded much faster.

When ties were present, only the Take The Best group answered more slowly; response times for the other groups were essentially unchanged. Because this shortcut requires checking additional traits only when top traits tie, the authors interpret this selective slowdown as evidence that the classifications capture real differences in mental processing, though they stop short of claiming the model directly observes thought.

“While we note that our findings were obtained (necessarily) in the context of a limited set of experiments, we do believe their theoretical and practical value has generalizability,” Banavar pointed out. “For instance, while the precise pervasiveness of heuristic usage is certainly context dependent, we still found that the simplest heuristic strategy was our most commonly classified strategy across all of our experiments, regardless of complexity manipulations. Our finding that strategy classifications are not fixed for individual people was also robust, and we have no reason to believe there would be within-person strategy variation only for our experiments and not for others.”

The researchers also investigated whether demographic characteristics predicted which strategy a person chose. Across variables such as race, gender, education, and political affiliation, associations were generally weak, and most were not statistically distinguishable from chance after adjusting for multiple tests. Older participants showed a slight tendency toward Take The Best, but the effect was small and held up after statistical correction in only 2 of 12 tests. Participants who rated a topic as less complex, or who said they knew less about it, also showed slight tendencies toward the shortcut, but these patterns appeared in only some analyses and largely did not survive correction.

“I was surprised by how difficult it was to relate strategy classification to respondent characteristics,” Banavar observed. “There’s a lot of evidence in cognitive science research showing that this is a difficult problem. There is also, however, substantial work in political science that would generate some predictions about relating strategy classification and respondent characteristics.”

“In the end we found very little, even though we considered demographics and various other measures of how meaningful a given political topic was to each person,” she said. “I think there’s a lot more to explore on this front.”

When the authors broke aggregate preferences down into individual weightings, they found that population-level averages concealed large differences. For every feature, many participants appeared to give it little or no weight, and for several of the most heavily weighted features, the pattern split into two sharp groups: people who effectively ignored the feature and a distinct group who weighted it very heavily. For example, conjoint studies commonly find that female candidates are slightly preferred over male candidates on average; the new results suggest this average blends people who prefer women, people who prefer men, and many who put little weight on gender at all.

As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study used simplified experimental profiles where each feature only had two possible choices, such as a candidate being either in their 50s or 70s. In real-world political decisions, options often have many more layers and continuous values, which might prompt respondents to rely even more heavily on mental shortcuts than observed here.

There are also important nuances in how mental shortcuts should be understood, especially regarding whether they reflect poorly on respondents. “First, the fact that we classify the majority of individuals as using heuristics or not using the rational strategy does not mean that they are lazy,” Banavar stressed. “We have finite resources and it is a good thing to selectively deploy them.”

The classification approach has its own limits. Because strategies were inferred from choices, someone who weighs every feature but cares overwhelmingly about one would make the same choices as a Take The Best user, and the model would classify them the same way; the response time data suggest such mix-ups were not widespread. Simulations also showed that the model tends to classify random guessers as Tally users, so guessing may be somewhat more common, and Tally somewhat less common, than the estimates suggest.

“Secondly, while we have built a cognitive model, the model doesn’t actually tell us what’s happening inside someone’s head,” Banavar stated. “It’s a model that classifies, based on the choices that people make, what decision strategies best describe their choices. It is a technical clarification but an important one.”

Future research could expand on this framework by testing features with more than two values, exploring why people pick the strategies they do, and modeling response times alongside choices.

text:
Hello MR Jethmalani ----Constitutional Authority Is Not Constitutional Infallibility. 

You have explained Article 324, the Representation of the People Act and the history of electoral-roll revisions. What you have conspicuously failed to explain is whether the Election Commission's exercise of those powers is beyond constitutional scrutiny. It is not.

Nobody disputes the Election Commission's constitutional status or its authority to revise electoral rolls. But constitutional authority does not mean unlimited authority. Every administrative action must satisfy constitutional guarantees, statutory requirements and principles of natural justice.

First, your historical argument is legally irrelevant. Merely because intensive electoral revisions have taken place since 1961 does not establish that every subsequent revision is constitutionally valid. An established administrative practice can still be challenged when its implementation violates the law.

Second, your claim about removing duplicate, deceased, migrated or ineligible voters avoids the actual constitutional question. Nobody is defending fraudulent registrations. The question is whether genuinely eligible citizens are being deprived of their electoral rights without adequate notice, proper verification and a meaningful opportunity to contest deletion.

In Lal Babu Hussein v. Electoral Registration Officer, (1995) 3 SCC 100, the Supreme Court intervened against electoral-roll deletion procedures, insisting upon compliance with natural justice. The Election Commission has been judicially corrected before.

In Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner, (1978) 1 SCC 405, the Supreme Court made clear that Article 324 powers operate within constitutional and statutory limitations. The Commission is not above the Constitution.

Third, your Seattle–New Jersey analogy is a diversion. Nobody advocates voting twice. Indian law itself prohibits multiple registrations under Sections 17 and 18 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950. But Section 22 also prescribes safeguards for deletion. Preventing duplicate registration and protecting eligible voters against wrongful deletion are complementary legal obligations, not contradictory ones.

Fourth, your Obama-era American comparison proves absolutely nothing about the legality of Indian electoral-roll revisions. The reported removal of 14.8 million US voter registrations does not, by itself, establish unlawful disenfranchisement in America. Equally, those American statistics cannot validate every electoral deletion undertaken in India. Each exercise must withstand scrutiny under its own laws.

Fifth, invoking Elon Musk's DOGE and Social Security records is another false equivalence. Administrative corrections to Social Security databases are not electoral-roll adjudications. A person appearing as deceased in one database does not automatically establish an unlawful voter registration or electoral fraud.

Sixth, and most importantly, who gave you the authority to decide who may question Indian democracy?

Article 19(1)(a) guarantees Indian citizens freedom of speech and expression. Article 19(1)(b) protects peaceful assembly. Article 21 safeguards life and personal liberty, including the dignity of persons within its constitutional protection.

Freedom of opinion and expression is also recognised internationally under Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

Whether someone belongs to the BJP, Congress, another political party, the legal profession, journalism or civil society—or speaks from India, Canada, America or elsewhere—does not disqualify that person from questioning an electoral authority. The constitutional rights enforceable within India may differ between citizens and foreign nationals, but nationality is no answer to legitimate criticism.

The Election Commission is an institution of constitutional accountability, not an institution entitled to unquestioning obedience.

The Constitution does not exist to protect the Election Commission from the people. It exists, among other purposes, to protect the people's democratic rights against unlawful exercises of public power.

So before delivering lectures about fake outrage and homework, understand one elementary principle:

Judicial scrutiny is not an insult to constitutional authority. Peaceful protest is not an attack on democracy. And questioning the Election Commission is not questioning the sovereignty of India.

Democracy belongs to the people—not to the temporary occupants of political office, nor to any constitutional authority claiming immunity from criticism. @RepJayapal

text:
Starlink has an Indian license, 20 ground stations on Indian soil, and a promise to keep Indian user data in India. What it doesn't have is permission to switch on.

Thousands of Indian villages still have no 4G. In the Northeast alone, more than 1,800 had no mobile signal of any kind as of February, most of them in Arunachal Pradesh. These are the places satellite internet is built for: mountain villages, islands, flood zones, anywhere a tower or a fiber line takes years and a lot of money to arrive.

Starlink has done what India asked. It got its telecom license in June 2025 and space regulator approval a month later. It built India-specific security controls, agreed to keep data local, and has been reporting the names, addresses and coordinates of its test terminals to the government every two weeks. It operates in more than 150 countries. In India it still can't sell a single subscription, and the company is now talking about early 2027.

New Delhi says nobody is being singled out, since Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's satellite venture are stuck at the same stage. I believe that, and I don't think it helps. When three licensed operators, two of them backed by India's biggest telecom groups, can't clear security review after more than a year of trials, that tells you the process has no deadline. It doesn't tell you it's thorough.

The security concerns are real. Indian agencies have been rattled by smuggled terminals turning up in border areas, and India is entitled to lawful interception, local data storage and an emergency shutoff. Starlink has already signed up for all of it. The answer to a misused terminal is enforcement, not keeping the service dark for everyone who would use it legally.

Elon Musk has been blunt, calling the delay "a crime against the people of India" and asking, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?" You don't need to buy the whole oligarch theory to see his point. Reliance spent months lobbying for spectrum auctions that would have favored deep-pocketed incumbents. The government sided with Starlink on that one, which is to its credit. Now it needs to finish the job.

India can keep every security power it wants and still let a kid in Arunachal get online. Right now it's choosing not to.

🚨MASSIVE: Russia Threatens Full-Scale Space War Against ELON MUSK, Puts all Starlink Satellites in the Crosshairs

Russia has issued increasingly sharp warnings over the use of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network in military operations against Russian territory. Moscow has suggested that if Starlink becomes directly involved in enabling deep strikes inside Russia, the satellites themselves could become targets.

The warning carries a far bigger implication than a dispute over internet connectivity.

Starlink has become deeply embedded in Ukraine’s wartime communications architecture, supporting battlefield communications, drone operations and the transmission of real-time information. As a result, Russia increasingly views the network not simply as civilian infrastructure, but as a strategic military enabler.

Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev has warned that attempts to interfere with Russia’s satellite capabilities could trigger what he described as a full-scale space war, while Russian officials have repeatedly threatened retaliation against systems supporting military operations.

Starlink has demonstrated that commercial satellite networks can become strategic infrastructure during wartime. The same technology that provides internet connectivity to remote communities can also support drones, command networks, battlefield communications and intelligence operations.

And that creates a fundamental vulnerability: whoever controls the network can potentially influence access to it.

India Cannot Build Its Digital Future Around a Foreign Network

For India, the lesson is not that Starlink should be rejected. The lesson is that Starlink cannot become India's only strategic option.

India can benefit enormously from satellite broadband, particularly in remote villages, difficult terrain, islands and areas where conventional fibre infrastructure is expensive or difficult to deploy. Foreign companies can bring capital, technology and competition to the Indian market.

But strategic dependence is an entirely different matter.

If a network is controlled by a foreign company operating within another country's geopolitical ecosystem, India cannot assume that access will remain uninterrupted during a future international crisis.

The Ukraine conflict has already demonstrated how satellite connectivity can become intertwined with military operations and geopolitical decisions. If access can be restricted because of a battlefield decision today, there is no guarantee that geopolitical pressure could not influence access tomorrow.

India therefore needs sovereign redundancy.

That means developing powerful domestic satellite constellations, secure satellite communications, indigenous ground infrastructure and the technological capability to operate independently when necessary.

text:
THE STARLINK QUESTION INDIA MUST ASK 🇮🇳

Why is Elon Musk pushing so aggressively to enter India’s satellite internet market?

Is this merely a business battle—or a question of DIGITAL SOVEREIGNTY?

FOLLOW THE MONEY. FOLLOW THE TECHNOLOGY.

Starlink is SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service. SpaceX also operates Starshield, a separate programme serving US national security customers.

In March 2024, Reuters reported a classified $1.8 BILLION contract involving SpaceX and America’s National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), an intelligence agency responsible for satellite-based reconnaissance.

The programme reportedly involves a network of satellites designed to enhance Earth observation and intelligence capabilities.

Reuters report:
https://t.co/IknOaaml55

Starlink and Starshield are NOT the same service. But both belong to the SpaceX ecosystem.

That raises legitimate strategic questions for every country considering foreign satellite infrastructure.

Who operates the network?
Who controls its software and updates?
Who governs access during a geopolitical crisis?
What happens when commercial interests collide with national interests?

These are questions of NATIONAL SECURITY, not anti-technology paranoia.

DATA IS THE NEW STRATEGIC TERRITORY.

Satellite internet can generate operational and subscriber information, including connection records and network metadata. Such information can have commercial value and, depending on the circumstances, potential intelligence value.

This does NOT prove that Starlink is handing Indian user data to US intelligence agencies.

But India must establish clear, enforceable safeguards for DATA PRIVACY, CYBERSECURITY and NATIONAL SECURITY before any foreign provider scales up.

ASK UKRAINE WHAT NETWORK DEPENDENCE CAN MEAN.

The Russia–Ukraine war has demonstrated how commercial satellite connectivity can become strategically important during a conflict.

When a private company controls a critical communications capability, its technical decisions can have consequences far beyond business.

India must ask a fundamental question: Can we maintain secure, uninterrupted communications when our national interests are at stake?

STRATEGIC AUTONOMY demands that we plan for that possibility.

INDIA IS NOT A TECHNOLOGICAL DESERT.

India has built a vast mobile communications ecosystem, expanded fibre connectivity and invested in indigenous telecom technology.

The answer is not to reject foreign technology automatically. It is to ensure that SATELLITE INTERNET complements India’s infrastructure without creating avoidable strategic dependencies.

REGULATION IS NOT THE SAME AS CONTROL.

A government can license a foreign company, impose security conditions and establish compliance requirements. But technical control also depends on network architecture, encryption, software access, operational authority and the ability to enforce national laws.

India needs independently verifiable safeguards, robust lawful-access procedures, incident-response mechanisms and credible contingency plans.

DIGITAL SOVEREIGNTY must be more than a policy slogan.

FAIR COMPETITION. EQUAL RULES. STRONG SECURITY.

India must not allow domestic monopolies to suppress innovation. Equally, commercial pressure must never weaken national security safeguards.

The real question is not whether India should welcome Starlink. Satellite internet could benefit millions of Indians. The question is whether any foreign company should become indispensable to critical Indian communications without strong sovereign safeguards.

Affordable connectivity.
Competition and innovation.
Indian data protection.
Secure infrastructure.
Enforceable regulatory oversight.

India must welcome technology on INDIAN TERMS.

THE BOTTOM LINE 🇮🇳

This is bigger than Elon Musk versus India’s telecom giants. India must never confuse access to technology with control over technology.

The 14-year-old boy police say was intentionally struck by a West Melbourne store owner last week has died, and the man accused of hitting him is now charged with second-degree murder.

With the family's consent, the West Melbourne Police Department has identified the teen as Hunter Russey of West Melbourne.

According to police, the case began around 4:30 a.m. on Tuesday, October 13, when 32-year-old Kavan Vishnubhai Patel, who owns the Corner Store at 100 South Wickham Road, received an alarm alert and saw on surveillance video that the store's front glass door had been broken. Patel told officers he saw someone leave the area on an e-bike.

Police say Patel followed the rider in his vehicle and intentionally struck him along Cocoanut Grove Avenue after the encounter at the store had ended. Investigators say Patel left Hunter on the side of the road without rendering aid, returned to the store, and did not tell responding officers he had hit him. Hunter was later found unresponsive in a roadside ditch.

Hunter was taken to Holmes Regional Medical Center as a trauma alert with severe injuries and was later transferred to Orlando Health Arnold Palmer Hospital for Children, where he remained on life support.

According to police, Hunter's family made the decision to remove him from life support on the evening of Saturday, October 17. He died at 11:46 p.m. His family has chosen to donate his organs to help others.

Patel was originally charged with aggravated battery and leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. Following Hunter's death, investigators obtained an arrest warrant, and Patel was rearrested just after 10 a.m. Sunday. He is now charged with second-degree murder and is being held at the Brevard County Jail without bond.

The West Melbourne Police Department offered condolences to Hunter's family and friends and said it will continue working the case and provide prosecutors with the evidence needed to move forward.

The family has asked that the public respect their privacy.

Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

text:
He won at the United States Supreme Court and four months later had to borrow ten dollars from his brother to buy a white shirt. Lloyd Gaines could not get hired anywhere in Missouri in 1939, quit a filling station job over a fuel scam, and was passing the hat at church meetings while the organization behind his case had spent twenty-five thousand dollars on it.

Sixteen days before he vanished, Lloyd Gaines wrote his mother that he wished nobody knew his name.

The letter is dated March 3, 1939. It sits today in a digital collection at the University of Missouri School of Law, the school that had spent three years refusing to let him through the door.

He told her his own people liked to applaud and shake his hand and pat him on the back and say how noble the idea was. Then, he wrote, it ended right there.

Off the newspaper pages, he told her, he was just a man. Not one who had fought and sacrificed to make the case possible, but one who was still fighting and still sacrificing, and nobody seemed to notice the difference.

He wrote that sometimes he wished he were a plain, ordinary man whose name no one recognized.

He had gone to Chicago, he explained, hoping to find it possible to make his own way. His room at the YMCA was paid through the seventh, and after that he would have to make other arrangements.

Then he closed the letter. If he forgot to write for a time, he told her, she should not worry, because he could look after himself.

Callie Gaines kept that letter. She was still holding on to the memory of it twelve years later, bedridden in an attic in St. Louis, when a magazine reporter climbed the stairs to ask her what had happened to her son.

Three months before he wrote it, Lloyd Gaines had won a case in the Supreme Court of the United States that is still taught in every constitutional law class in this country.

Start where he started, because the distance he covered is the whole point.

He was born in 1911 in Water Valley, Mississippi, to a tenant farmer named Henry Gaines and his wife Callie. There were eleven children, and several of them died while Lloyd was small, and so did his father.

In the spring of 1926, Callie brought what was left of her family north to St. Louis to live with her oldest son George. It was the same road hundreds of thousands of Black families were taking in those years, out of the cotton counties and into the cities.

Lloyd was fifteen years old. When St. Louis tested what Mississippi had taught him, the city put him in the fifth grade at Waring Elementary School.

Sit with that a moment. A boy of fifteen, a head taller than every child in the room, folding himself into a desk built for a ten year old.

He did not walk out. He caught up.

By high school he was on the debate team at Vashon and writing for the school journal, and his class elected him a senior officer. He graduated in 1931, and an essay he wrote won him a two hundred fifty dollar scholarship.

That money was not enough, so at Lincoln University in Jefferson City he sold magazines on the street to cover the rest. He was elected president of his senior class, he joined Alpha Phi Alpha, and in 1935 he took a history degree with honors.

Eleven years earlier he had been a fifteen year old in the fifth grade. Now he wanted to be a lawyer.

There was exactly one problem, and it was the whole state of Missouri.

Lincoln was the state's college for Black students and it had no law school. The University of Missouri had one, and it was for white students only, and Missouri's answer to that arrangement was a scholarship program that would pay a Black student to go be a lawyer in somebody else's state.

In June of 1935, Gaines wrote to the registrar's office in Columbia and asked for a catalog and an application form.

They mailed him both without hesitating. The form had no line on it asking a man his race, so nobody in that office had any idea who they were writing to.

He filled it out and sent it back that August. The registrar, S. W. Canada, did not admit him and did not reject him, because he did not yet know there was anything to think about.

Then Gaines's transcript arrived from Lincoln University, and Canada understood.

He left the application sitting on his desk. He did nothing with it at all, and he sent Gaines a telegram suggesting he come in and discuss a possible arrangement instead.

Gaines wrote to the president of the University of Missouri directly, asking to be admitted. Frederick Middlebush never answered him.

By March of 1936 the denial was formal and in writing, and the board's position was that segregation was the public policy of the state and Gaines could go be educated somewhere else at Missouri's expense.

On April 15, 1936, he sued.

The trial opened on July 10, 1936, in the Boone County courthouse in Columbia, and the heat that morning was already climbing past a hundred degrees.

That was the summer of the great drought, and white farmers had come in from the surrounding country to file for relief. Some of them drifted into the courtroom out of curiosity, because they had lived their whole lives in Missouri and had never once seen Black attorneys argue a case.

A hundred law students packed in to watch. Reporters filled the rest.

Almost no local Black residents came. There had been two lynchings in the area not long before, and people had done the arithmetic on what it might cost to be seen sitting in that room on that day.

The courtroom itself had no separate section, so the few who did come sat mixed in with everybody else. Judge W. M. Dinwiddie looked at the crowd and the windows and suggested the lawyers take their jackets off.

Charles Hamilton Houston sat at the same table as the attorneys for the state, and both sides shook hands before it began. Within an hour he was dismantling them.

Gaines took the stand first. He said he wanted Missouri's law school because it was a good one, and because Columbia was closer to his mother's house in St. Louis than the law schools of Iowa or Illinois or Kansas.

He also pointed out that the University of Missouri took students from other states, and had taken students from as far away as India, and that he was a Missouri taxpayer.

The state's lawyer, William Hogsett, went after him on cross-examination with one line of attack. He wanted the record to show that Gaines had no real interest in practicing law and was only there to be a plaintiff.

When had he first contacted the NAACP, and had he ever seen a Black student on that campus. Did he not already know Black students were never admitted.

Gaines said he had not known.

Then Houston called the law school's own dean, William Masterson, as a hostile witness, and took him apart in front of the room.

Masterson testified there was no special advantage to studying Missouri law at Missouri, since all the neighboring schools used the same casebooks. Houston reminded him that his own law review had a standing policy of publishing an article on Missouri law in every single issue.

Houston then handed him the University of Iowa's catalog, which advertised exactly that advantage to students who wanted to practice in Iowa. The dean held his position anyway.

On cross-examination the dean of a law school could not recall how his admissions process worked or what his budget was, and could not say whether his was the only public law school in the state of Missouri.

Houston wrote later that he had never in his career watched a man's memory fail him so completely.

A state senator named F. M. McDavid, who chaired the Board of Curators, testified that admitting one Black student would be disruptive and would undo a hundred years of tradition. He added that it would be very unhappy for Gaines personally.

Houston asked him whether he really believed a tradition could bind progress forever. Then he asked whether McDavid knew of any trouble caused at Maryland, which had admitted a Black law student the year before, and McDavid admitted he had never looked into it.

Robert Witherspoon, a Black attorney practicing in St. Louis, testified plainly that being forced out of state for his own legal education had put him behind for the rest of his career.

Two weeks later Judge Dinwiddie ruled for the state. He did not write an opinion explaining why.

The Missouri Supreme Court took it up next, and the case was considered important enough that all seven justices heard it instead of the usual division.

On December 9, 1937, they ruled against him unanimously. Justice William Francis Frank wrote that a state's right to separate the races in education was no longer an open question, and that what the law promised every citizen was equality, not identity.

Three of those seven judges had graduated from the law school Gaines was trying to enter. So had the trial judge.

On November 9, 1938, Houston stood up in the Supreme Court of the United States and argued that no amount of Missouri's money spent in another state could buy Gaines an equal education.

The decision came down thirty-three days later, on December 12, 1938. Six to two.

Chief Justice Charles Evans Hughes wrote that the question was not what other states offered, but what Missouri offered white students and denied Black students for no reason but color. Paying a man's tuition somewhere else, he wrote, does not remove the discrimination.

Understand what that did. Fourteen other states were running the same out-of-state scholarship scheme, and in one afternoon every one of them lost it.

From that day forward a segregated state had two choices and only two. Integrate the school it already had, or build a second one, brick for brick, faculty for faculty, for a handful of Black students.

Houston had bet everything on states doing the arithmetic and choosing to integrate, because duplication was ruinously expensive.

Missouri chose the bricks.

The legislature moved with a speed it had never once shown on behalf of Black Missourians. It appropriated two hundred seventy five thousand dollars, Governor Lloyd Stark signed the bill, and the state leased an old beauty college at 4310 St. Ferdinand Avenue in the Ville, in St. Louis.

Poro Beauty College became the Lincoln University School of Law. Thirty-one students enrolled that first term, and pickets stood on the sidewalk outside calling the whole thing what it was.

Frank M. Jones of the Colored Clerks Circle said publicly that the new school was a farce and was inferior in every respect.

Meanwhile the Missouri Supreme Court, ordered to rehear the case, pushed the hearing back to May of 1939. That delay conveniently kept every Black applicant out of the University of Missouri for the remainder of the school year.

In January of 1939, a young managing editor at the Kansas City Call named Lucile Bluford applied to the University of Missouri's graduate journalism program and was accepted by mail. She traveled to Columbia to register, and they took one look at her and turned her away.

The registrar who did it was the same S. W. Canada. He told her the Gaines matter had not been finally decided and he did not know yet what he was supposed to do.

She sued. She tried to enroll eleven separate times, and when a court finally left Missouri no way out, the university shut down its entire graduate journalism program rather than seat her.

Now look at what was happening to Gaines himself during those same months, because this is the part that gets skipped.

He came back to Missouri in early 1939 with a master's degree in economics from the University of Michigan and his name on a decision of the United States Supreme Court. He could not get hired.

He took work at a filling station. He quit it when he realized the owner was pumping low grade fuel into the high grade tank, because a fraud charge was the one thing he could not survive.

He gave speeches to NAACP chapters and church congregations and asked for donations at the end of them. He told those rooms he was ready, willing and able to enroll in September.

To get to a speaking engagement in Kansas City he had to borrow ten dollars from his brother George so he could buy himself a white shirt.

That is the arithmetic of it. The organization behind the case had spent twenty-five thousand dollars on it, and the man whose name was on it needed ten dollars from his brother to look presentable while talking about it.

On February 27, 1939, he spoke at Sumner High School in St. Louis to a crowded auditorium full of young people.

The man who introduced him, Dr. S. H. Thompson, told that audience Gaines was a hero, probably, or a martyr, maybe, a man who had given himself in sacrifice for his people. He said it as praise, three weeks before it came true.

Then Gaines stood up in front of those children and told them to choose a goal, and that success would be theirs.

Choose one so high you cannot reach out and grasp it, he told them, one as clear as the stars above. Follow it, he said, even though you may never reach it.

Four days later he sat down and wrote the letter to his mother.

Privately, it was already over. Callie Gaines said afterward that the two of them had reached an understanding that he was not going to enroll, because they both believed it was too dangerous.

The family believed threats had reached them, and the descendants still believe it. People who came up around Water Valley, Mississippi, did not take threats like that to the police, because they knew exactly how much protection that would buy.

Nancy Page, an old neighbor from the Central West End who was feeding him dinner in Chicago that spring, finally asked him straight out whether he was going through with it.

He did not answer her straight. He said something to the effect that if he did not go, he would at least have made it possible for some other boy or girl to go.

She said later that in those last days he seemed to be running away from something. She never asked him what, out of respect for his privacy.

March 19, 1939, was a Sunday in Chicago, cold and wet.

His money at the YMCA had run out on the seventh, so he was staying at an Alpha Phi Alpha house, where his fraternity brothers had passed a hat for him. He had told Nancy Page he had taken a job at a department store, and a reporter later confirmed he had indeed been hired and had never shown up for the first shift.

He had promised the Page family he would take them out to dinner that night. They had been feeding him for weeks and this was how he meant to settle it.

Early that evening, he told the house attendant he was going out to buy stamps.

He left his duffel bag at the fraternity house with his clothes still in it, dirty laundry and all. A man who has decided to disappear on purpose does not leave his laundry on the floor.

Nobody who knew him ever saw him again.

Here is the part that should stop you. Nobody reported it.

Not the fraternity brothers, not the Pages, not his family in St. Louis, not his lawyers, not the organization that had built its entire national legal strategy on his name. He had a long habit of traveling without telling anyone, so for weeks and then months his silence looked ordinary.

In August, Houston and Sidney Redmond went looking for him to take depositions for the rehearing, and could not find him.

In late September the law school Missouri had built to avoid him opened its doors and thirty-one students walked in. He was not one of them.

On October 11, 1939, the Columbia Missourian ran it on the front page. Gaines missing, and the case might die with him.

That was seven months after the stamps.

In January of 1940 the state of Missouri moved to dismiss the suit for want of a plaintiff. Houston and Redmond did not oppose the motion, and the court granted it.

The most important desegregation ruling in America before Brown ended in a Missouri courtroom because the man it belonged to could not be produced.

J. Edgar Hoover put it in writing that year that he did not consider the disappearance a federal matter. Somebody wrote to ask him again thirty years later and received the same answer.

The NAACP had nothing left. Twenty-five thousand dollars was gone, Houston was ill with the tuberculosis that would kill him a decade later, and new plaintiffs were nearly impossible to find in a Depression.

The University of Missouri did not admit its first Black students until 1950, eleven years after the stamps, and only because it was sued again.

In May of 1951, Ebony magazine sent a reporter named Edward T. Clayton to find out what had become of Lloyd Gaines.

He climbed to that attic room and found Callie Gaines. She told him about the last thing she ever received from her son, a postcard telling her goodbye, and that if she did not hear from him anymore she would know he was all right.

She had heard every rumor by then, Mexico, New York, a payoff from somebody. She told Clayton that nobody knew any more than she did.

George was not gentle with Clayton. He said the organization had his brother out making speeches all over the state, and that when Lloyd needed to get to Kansas City it was George who handed him the money for a shirt.

Lloyd owed his brother five hundred dollars when he walked out for the stamps.

Redmond conceded years later that the family had never seemed eager to help find him, and he understood why. They believed the movement had put their boy out in front of the whole state and then left him standing there alone.

In the late 1940s, Lorenzo Greene, Gaines's old mentor at Lincoln, said he made contact with him in Mexico City. Greene claimed he spoke to him by telephone several times and recognized the voice instantly, and that they made a plan to have dinner, and that Gaines never came.

Greene never reported any of it to the FBI. His son explained why in one sentence, which was that there was not a lot of trust there.

The family is still split. One great-niece has said she would rather believe he lived a full life in Mexico than think about the alternative.

Another, Tracy Berry, who grew up to become a federal prosecutor, has said she cannot reconcile that with the man she was told about. If he wanted to walk away, she has pointed out, there were easier ways than cutting off every person who loved him.

The FBI finally accepted the file in 2007. It was the oldest case on the list.

Now look at the two ledgers side by side.

Missouri's ledger shows a scholarship fund established in 1995, a Black culture center carrying his name, a portrait hanging in a prominent spot in the law school building, an honorary law degree in 2006, and a posthumous license to practice law signed off by the same court that had ruled against him sixty-nine years earlier.

If he had walked into that building in 2006 at the age of ninety-five and asked for a case to try, the paperwork was in order.

His family's ledger shows a monument they put up in a Missouri cemetery in 1999 with nothing underneath it, and no death certificate, because they have never asked for one. One of his sisters went to her own grave still believing he was alive somewhere.

Missouri's version of this story ends on a courthouse step in December of 1938, and it is a very good story that way.

His mother's version ends in an attic with a postcard, and that one is true too.

Three weeks before he walked out into the cold, Lloyd Gaines stood in a school auditorium and told a room full of children to pick a goal so high they could not close their hands around it, and to follow it even if they never reached it.

He was describing his own life and he did not know it yet. The second half of that sentence is the part Missouri left off the plaque, and somebody has to keep it attached to his name.

Lloyd Gaines changed the course of American education, but the mystery of what happened to him remains one of the great unfinished stories in civil rights history. I research forgotten stories like his because the people who carried the weight of history deserve to be remembered. If you want to support this work:
https://t.co/Vm6JEQzdIW
Every coffee helps keep these lost histories alive.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal.  Police argued the content insulted the Election Commission, undermined its integrity and transparency, spread false claims about a rectified clerical error, and risked public order or communal harmony by potentially fuelling political division. Reports indicated hundreds of accounts were flagged (approximately 270 on X, 200 on Facebook, and 90 on Instagram). The .IN Registry took https://t.co/6D4RZacQWP off the internet three days after it went live, without notice or reasons. The site was a fully sourced, non-commercial record of the NEET paper-leak protests and the “Chalo Sansad” march. On 14 October 2026, the Delhi High Court issued notice in Sriram Viswanathan v. National Internet Exchange of India & Ors. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/IObo9F6mNB

Indian law already prescribes how online content may be blocked. Section 69A of the IT Act and the 2009 Blocking Rules require a written order, reasons, committee review and a hearing. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in Shreya Singhal (2015) because of these safeguards, and none were followed here. NIXI now says it will examine every .IN domain using “Sansad” or “Parliament”, acting on a private legal opinion and without any statutory power. (6/7)

Counsel for NIXI, MeitY, the Department of Consumer Affairs and GoDaddy appeared before Justice Amit Mahajan, and the matter will next be heard on 27 January 2027. The petition seeks restoration of the domain and disclosure of the legal opinion. It also asks that NIXI give prior notice, reasons and a hearing before suspending any .IN domain. If your .IN domain has been suspended without notice or reasons, write to us. (7/7)
